source_refs.note: Chapter 10 exercise (PDF 246-250, printed 243-247): MCQs keyed from the chapter (the book prints no key), model answers to the written questions, numericals worked step by step and checked against the printed answers; corrections in the lesson.

blocks.prompt: 10.1 A current is flowing towards north along a power line. The direction of the magnetic field over the wire is directed towards:
blocks.explanation: Right-hand grip rule: grip the wire with the thumb pointing north (along the current); the fingers curl over the top of the wire towards the west. So above the wire the field points west.

blocks.prompt: 10.2 The radius of curvature of the path of a charged particle in a uniform magnetic field is directly proportional to:

options.text: the flux density of the field

blocks.explanation: The magnetic force provides the centripetal force: qvB = mv²/r, so r = mv/(qB) = p/(qB). r ∝ momentum.

blocks.prompt: 10.3 The diagram shows a beam of electrons entering a magnetic field. What is the effect of magnetic field on the electrons? [Printed diagram: the beam of electrons moves to the right; the magnetic field lines are vertical, pointing down the page.]

options.text: They are deflected into the plane of the diagram.
They are deflected out of the plane of the diagram.
They are deflected towards the bottom of the diagram.
They are deflected towards the top of the diagram.

blocks.explanation: F = qv × B. For a positive charge, v (right) × B (down) points into the page. The electron is negative, so the force is reversed: out of the plane of the diagram. (The force is perpendicular to both v and B, so it cannot be up or down the page.)

blocks.prompt: 10.4 The force exerted on a wire of 1 metre length carrying 1 ampere current placed at right angle to the magnetic field is called:
blocks.explanation: From F = BIL, B = F/IL: B is numerically the force on a 1 m conductor carrying 1 A at right angles to the field. B is called magnetic induction (magnetic field strength, flux density).

blocks.prompt: 10.5 The unit of flux density is:
blocks.explanation: B = F/IL, so 1 T = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹ (= 1 Wb m⁻²).

blocks.prompt: 10.6 A moving charged particle is surrounded by:
blocks.explanation: Every charge has an electric field; a moving charge is also a current, so it produces a magnetic field as well.

blocks.prompt: 10.7 Magnetic force on the charge q moving parallel to magnetic field with velocity v is:
blocks.explanation: F = qvB sinθ; moving parallel to the field θ = 0°, sin 0° = 0, so F = 0.

blocks.prompt: 10.8 The unit N A⁻¹ m⁻¹ is called:
blocks.explanation: 1 tesla = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹, the unit of magnetic induction B. (The weber, N m A⁻¹, is the unit of flux.)

blocks.prompt: 10.9 Electrons while moving perpendicularly through a uniform magnetic field are:
blocks.explanation: The force qvB is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it acts as a centripetal force and the electrons move in a circle (r = mv/eB).

blocks.prompt: 10.10 A magnet is suspended from a spring. The magnet oscillates and moves in and out of the coil connected to a galvanometer. When the magnet oscillates, the galvanometer shows:

options.text: deflection to the left and to the right with constant amplitude
deflection to the left and right, but the amplitude steadily decreases

blocks.explanation: Moving in and out changes the flux in opposite senses, so the induced current reverses (left and right deflection). By Lenz's law the induced current opposes the motion, taking energy from the oscillation, so the amplitude of the oscillation and of the deflection steadily decreases.

blocks.prompt: 10.1 It is said that Lenz's law specifically applies to induced currents and not directly to induce emf. Explain it briefly.
blocks.explanation: Lenz's law says the induced current opposes the change that caused it; the opposition comes from the magnetic field (or force) of that current. An emf in an open circuit drives no current, so nothing opposes the change. So Lenz's law is applied to a closed loop (or the loop is imagined closed) to find the direction of the current, and the polarity of the emf is inferred from it.

blocks.prompt: 10.2 A square loop of wire is moving through a uniform magnetic field. The normal to the loop is oriented parallel to the magnetic field. Is an emf induced in the loop? Give a reason for your answer.
blocks.explanation: No. The flux through the loop is φ = BA cos 0° = BA. While the loop moves through a uniform field (without rotating or leaving the field), B, A and the angle stay the same, so the flux does not change and no emf is induced.

blocks.prompt: 10.3 Does the induced emf always act to decrease the magnetic flux through a circuit?
blocks.explanation: No. The induced emf (current) opposes the change in flux, not the flux itself. If the flux is increasing it tries to decrease it; if the flux is decreasing it tries to increase (maintain) it.

blocks.prompt: 10.4 When a magnet is pushed into the solenoid, as shown in the figure (a), the galvanometer indicates a small current. Why is the current produced? What will be the magnetic pole produced at the left end of the solenoid? [Figure (a): a bar magnet hangs from a spring with its N pole up and its S pole entering the end of the coil, which is joined to a galvanometer.]
blocks.explanation:
Pushing the magnet in increases the magnetic flux through the solenoid. By Faraday's law a changing flux induces an emf, which drives a current through the closed circuit.
By Lenz's law the end of the solenoid facing the magnet must repel the approaching pole. The magnet's S pole is entering, so that end (the end the book calls the left end) becomes a south pole.

blocks.prompt: 10.5 A bar magnet falls through a fixed metal ring (Fig b). Will the magnet fall with an acceleration of a freely falling body? Give reason.
blocks.explanation: No, its acceleration is less than g. As the magnet falls, the flux through the ring changes and a current is induced in the ring. By Lenz's law this current opposes the motion (it repels the magnet as it approaches and attracts it as it leaves), so an upward force acts on the magnet.

blocks.prompt: 10.6 Which of the two charged particles of the same mass will be deflected most in the magnetic field (a) fast moving (b) slow moving?
blocks.explanation: (b) The slow moving one (taking equal charges). The radius of its circular path is r = mv/(qB); smaller v gives a smaller radius, i.e., a more sharply curved path, so it is deflected more.

blocks.prompt: 10.7 An electron and a proton are projected into a magnetic field at right angles to it with a certain velocity. Which of the particles will suffer greater deflection? Why?
blocks.explanation: The electron. Both have the same magnitude of charge e and the same v, so r = mv/(eB) ∝ m. The electron's mass is about 1/1836 of the proton's, so its path has a much smaller radius and it is deflected more (and in the opposite direction).

blocks.prompt: 10.8 Can a single moving proton produce magnetic field?
blocks.explanation: Yes. A moving charge is an electric current, and every current produces a magnetic field around it. So a single moving proton is surrounded by both an electric and a magnetic field (a proton at rest has only an electric field).

blocks.prompt: 10.9 A magnetic field is necessary if there is to be a magnetic flux passing through a coil of wire. Yet, just because there is a magnetic field does not mean that a magnetic flux will pass through a coil. Account for this situation.
blocks.explanation: Flux is φ = BA cos θ, where θ is the angle between B and the normal to the coil. If the plane of the coil is parallel to the field (θ = 90°), cos 90° = 0, so no flux passes through the coil even though the field is present. Flux depends on the orientation (and area) as well as on B.

blocks.prompt: 10.1 A charge is lying stationary between the opposite poles of two magnets. Is a magnetic force exerted on it? Why?
blocks.explanation: No. The magnetic force on a charge is F = qvB sin θ. For a stationary charge v = 0, so F = 0. A magnetic field exerts a force only on a moving charge (the field is the same on both sides, and no electric field acts here).

blocks.prompt: 10.2 When the switch in the circuit is closed, a current is established in the coil and the metal ring jumps upward. Why? Describe what would happen to the ring if the battery polarity were reversed. [Figure: a metal ring rests on top of a vertical coil wound on an iron core; the coil is connected to a battery through switch S.]
blocks.explanation:
On closing the switch the current in the coil grows from zero, so the magnetic flux through the ring increases suddenly. By Faraday's law an emf and a current are induced in the ring. By Lenz's law the ring's current opposes the increase of flux, so it flows opposite to the coil current; the ring then acts like a magnet with like pole facing the coil, and the coil repels it. The ring jumps up.
If the battery polarity is reversed, the ring still jumps up: the coil's field is reversed, but the flux through the ring still increases from zero, so the induced current again opposes it and is again opposite to the coil current. Opposite currents repel whatever the direction.

blocks.prompt: 10.3 The figure shows a coil of wire in the x – y plane with a magnetic field directed along the y-axis. Around which of the three-coordinate axis should the coil be rotated in order to generate an emf and a current in the coil?
blocks.explanation:
Around the x-axis.
The coil lies in the x–y plane, so its normal is along the z-axis, perpendicular to B (along y): the flux is zero at the start.
- Rotating about the x-axis tilts the normal towards the y-axis, so the angle between B and the normal changes, the flux changes and an emf and current are induced.
- Rotating about the y-axis keeps the normal in the x–z plane, always perpendicular to B, so the flux stays zero.
- Rotating about the z-axis keeps the coil in the x–y plane, so the flux stays zero.

blocks.prompt: 10.4 Is it possible to change both the area of the loop and the magnetic field passing through the loop and still not have an induced emf in the loop? Give reason.
blocks.explanation: Yes. An emf is induced only when the flux φ = BA cos θ changes. If B and A are changed together so that their product stays constant (for example the area is doubled while B is halved at the same time), the flux does not change and no emf is induced.

blocks.prompt: 10.5 Does the application of uniform magnetic field to a moving charged particle result in a change in kinetic energy of the particle? Explain.
blocks.explanation: No. The magnetic force F = q(v × B) is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work (W = Fd cos 90° = 0). It changes only the direction of motion, not the speed, so the kinetic energy ½mv² stays the same.

blocks.prompt: 10.6 A uniform electric field and a magnetic field act in the same direction. A proton is projected, into the space, with a uniform velocity in opposite direction. What will happen to the proton?
blocks.explanation:
Magnetic force: the velocity is anti-parallel to B (θ = 180°), so F = qvB sin 180° = 0; the magnetic field has no effect.
Electric force: F = qE acts on the proton along E, i.e., opposite to its velocity. So the proton slows down (decelerates) in a straight line, stops for an instant, and then accelerates back along the direction of E. It is not deflected sideways.

blocks.prompt: 10.7 A conductor moves in a magnetic field when a current is passed through the conductor. Would you expect the reverse effect to occur? That is, would a current be produced if a conductor is moved across the magnetic field?
blocks.explanation: Yes. When a conductor is moved across a magnetic field, a motional emf ε = vBL is induced between its ends (electromagnetic induction). If the conductor is part of a closed circuit, this emf drives a current. This is the principle of the generator, the reverse of the motor effect.

blocks.prompt: 10.8 Consider a conducting rod of length L moving with velocity v to the right as shown in the figure. Left ends of the conducting rails are connected to a bulb. Due to motion of the rod through the magnetic field, an emf is produced across the ends of the rod. This emf gives rise to a current I. As a result, the bulb lights up. Explain where does the electrical energy consumed by the bulb come from? [Figure: the magnetic field B is into the page; the rod slides to the right on two rails a distance d apart.]
blocks.explanation:
From the work done by the external agent that pulls the rod.
The induced current I in the rod flows in the magnetic field, so the rod feels a magnetic force F = ILB. By Lenz's law this force is opposite to the velocity and tends to stop the rod. To keep the rod moving at constant velocity, an external force equal to ILB must be applied in the direction of motion. The mechanical work done by this force is converted into electrical energy (P = Fv = ILBv = Iε), which the bulb changes into light and heat. This agrees with the law of conservation of energy.

blocks.prompt: 10.9 What will you do if you want to save a sensitive instrument from stray magnetic fields?
blocks.explanation: Enclose the instrument in a box made of soft iron (or another high-permeability material such as mu-metal). The magnetic field lines prefer to pass through the iron walls and go round the inside, so the space inside the box is almost free of magnetic field (magnetic shielding).

blocks.prompt: 10.1 Distinguish between magnetic flux and flux density. How are they related?
blocks.explanation: Magnetic flux is the number of field lines through an area; flux density is the flux per unit area held perpendicular to the field. They are related by φ = B·A = BA cos θ, so B = φ/A when the area is perpendicular to the field.

rows: Number of magnetic field lines passing through a given area
Number of field lines per unit area held perpendicular to the field
B = φ/A (area perpendicular to the field); B = F/IL
Vector quantity, in the direction of the field
Unit: tesla (T) = Wb m⁻² = N A⁻¹ m⁻¹
Depends on B, the area and its orientation
Describes the strength of the field at a point

blocks.prompt: 10.2 Find an expression for the force exerted on a current-carrying conductor placed in a uniform magnetic field.
blocks.explanation:
When a current-carrying conductor is placed in a magnetic field, its own field interacts with the external field: on one side the two fields reinforce, on the other they cancel, and the conductor is pushed towards the weaker side.
Experimentally the force F on a straight conductor placed perpendicular to a uniform field is directly proportional to:
1. the current I: F ∝ I
2. the length L of the conductor in the field: F ∝ L
3. the magnetic field strength B: F ∝ B
Combining: F ∝ BIL, or F = kBIL. In SI units k = 1, so
F = BIL (conductor perpendicular to B)
This also defines B = F/IL, unit tesla, 1 T = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹.
If the conductor makes an angle θ with B, only the component L sin θ perpendicular to B is effective:
F = BIL sin θ
In vector form (L along the current): F = I L × B
Special cases: F is maximum, BIL, when θ = 90°; F = 0 when the conductor is along the field (θ = 0°).
Direction: F is perpendicular to both L and B, given by Fleming's left-hand rule (first finger along the field, second finger along the current, thumb gives the force) or the right-hand rule (curl the fingers from I to B, the thumb gives F).

blocks.prompt: 10.3 State and explain Faraday's law and Lenz's law. Also describe factors affecting the induced emf.
blocks.explanation:
Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction:
The average emf induced in a conducting coil of N loops is equal to the negative of the rate at which the magnetic flux through the coil is changing with time:
ε = −N Δφ/Δt
Explanation: a rod of length L moves with velocity v along two rails in a field B (into the page), forming a closed loop. The motional emf is ε = −vBL. In time Δt the rod moves Δx = vΔt, so the area of the loop increases by ΔA = LΔx and the flux by Δφ = BLΔx. Then ε = −BLΔx/Δt = −Δφ/Δt for one loop, and for N loops ε = −NΔφ/Δt. This result is true in general, for any change of flux.

Lenz's law:
The direction of the induced current is always such that it opposes the change that caused it. (This is the meaning of the minus sign in Faraday's law.)
Explanation: when the N pole of a bar magnet is pushed towards a coil, the induced current makes the face of the coil towards the magnet a north pole, which repels the magnet (the current is anticlockwise as seen from the magnet). When the magnet is pulled away, that face becomes a south pole and attracts it.
Lenz's law and conservation of energy: for the sliding rod, the induced current gives a force F = ILB opposite to the velocity, so work must be done to keep the rod moving; this work becomes electrical energy. If the current flowed the other way, the force would speed the rod up and energy would be created from nothing, which is impossible. So Lenz's law is a consequence of the law of conservation of energy.

Factors affecting the induced emf:
1. Rate of change of magnetic flux: the faster the flux changes, the greater the emf.
2. Number of turns of the coil: emf ∝ N; more turns, more emf.
3. Relative speed of the coil (or conductor) and the field: a faster speed changes the flux faster and increases the emf.
(The strength of the field and the area of the coil also matter, because they decide how much flux changes.)

blocks.prompt: 10.4 Determine the force acting on a charged particle moving through a uniform magnetic field.
blocks.explanation:
A current is a flow of charges, so each moving charge in a magnetic field experiences a force. Start from the force on a current-carrying conductor.
1. Let N particles, each of charge q, pass through a conductor of length L in time t. The current is I = Nq/t.
2. If v is their velocity along the conductor, t = L/v, so I = Nqv/L ... (1)
3. Force on the conductor in a uniform field B: F = I L × B, with L = L L̂ (L̂ the unit vector along the current).
4. Substituting (1): F = (Nqv/L)(L L̂ × B) = Nqv L̂ × B
5. Since the velocity is along the conductor, v = v L̂, so F = Nq v × B
6. This is the force on N particles, so the force on one particle is
F = q v × B
Magnitude: F = qvB sin θ, where θ is the angle between v and B.
- Maximum force qvB when v is perpendicular to B (θ = 90°).
- Zero force when v is along B (θ = 0° or 180°), and zero for a charge at rest.
Direction: perpendicular to both v and B (right-hand rule or Fleming's left-hand rule); for a negative charge it is reversed. A positive charge entering a field directed into the paper is deflected one way (for example upward) and a negative charge the opposite way along a curved path. Because F is perpendicular to v, it changes only the direction of motion, not the speed.

blocks.prompt: 10.5 What is a velocity selector? Explain its working.
blocks.explanation:
Velocity selector: a device in which electric and magnetic forces act on a moving charged particle in such a way that they balance each other for only one value of velocity, so particles of only that velocity pass straight through.
Construction: a cylindrical tube placed in a uniform magnetic field B (into the paper). Inside the tube is a parallel-plate capacitor that produces a uniform electric field E perpendicular to B. The particle enters with velocity v perpendicular to both E and B.
Working: for a positive charge +q:
- magnetic force F_B = qvB, upward;
- electric force F_E = qE, downward (along E).
E and B are adjusted so that the two forces cancel. With no net force, the particle moves in a straight line with constant velocity (Newton's first law) and leaves through the exit at the right end of the tube.
Condition: qvB = qE, so
v = E/B
Particles faster than E/B have a larger magnetic force and are deflected one way; slower particles are deflected the other way, so they do not come out of the exit. Thus only particles of velocity v = E/B are selected, whatever their charge or mass.

blocks.prompt: 10.6 Explain how ferrofluids work?
blocks.explanation:
Ferrofluid: a material that shows both liquid and magnetic properties.
Composition: a colloidal suspension of magnetic nanoparticles (usually iron oxide, about 10 nm in size) in a carrier fluid such as oil or water. The particles are coated with a surfactant, which reduces surface tension and stops them from clumping, so they stay evenly spread. The viscosity of the fluid, the tiny size of the particles and their constant motion stop them from settling.
Working:
1. With no magnet nearby, the ferrofluid behaves like an ordinary liquid.
2. When a magnet is brought near, the particles are temporarily magnetized and the fluid itself becomes a magnet; the particles form chain-like structures along the field lines, which increase the viscosity, so the fluid acts more like a solid.
3. The shape depends on a competition between magnetic forces, surface tension and gravity. Where the magnetic forces overcome the others, the fluid bulges into sharp spikes along the field lines.
4. When the magnet is removed, the particles are demagnetized and the fluid becomes an ordinary liquid again.
Simple experiment: mix laser-printer toner (about 40% iron oxide nanoparticles) with cooking oil in a bottle; bring a magnet near and the fluid jumps towards it and forms spikes.
Applications: rotary seals in computer hard drives and motors; cooling and damping the voice coil of loudspeakers; targeted drug delivery directed by external magnets; contrast agents in MRI; damping and control of liquid flow.

blocks.prompt: 10.1 A positively charged particle is projected perpendicularly into a magnetic field at a speed of 1500 m s⁻¹. It experiences a force of magnitude F. At what angle θ with the field, the particle should be projected at a speed of 2000 m s⁻¹, so that it experiences the same magnitude of force? (Ans: θ = 49°)
blocks.explanation:
Given: v₁ = 1500 m s⁻¹ at θ₁ = 90°; v₂ = 2000 m s⁻¹; same F, same q and B
Required: θ = ?
Solution:
F = qvB sin θ
qv₁B sin 90° = qv₂B sin θ
sin θ = v₁/v₂ = 1500/2000 = 0.75
θ = sin⁻¹(0.75) = 48.6° ≈ 49°
Answer: θ ≈ 49°

blocks.prompt: 10.2 Electrons are accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 15 kV in an oscilloscope. The electrons then pass through a 0.35 T magnetic field that deflects them to the desired position on the screen. Find the magnitude of the maximum force that an electron can experience. (Ans: 4.1 × 10⁻¹² N)
blocks.explanation:
Given: V = 15 kV = 1.5 × 10⁴ V; B = 0.35 T; e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg
Required: F_max = ?
Solution:
Speed gained: ½mv² = eV
v = √(2eV/m) = √(2 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1.5 × 10⁴/9.1 × 10⁻³¹) = √(5.27 × 10¹⁵) = 7.26 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹
The force is maximum when v is perpendicular to B (sin 90° = 1):
F_max = evB = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)(7.26 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹)(0.35 T) = 4.07 × 10⁻¹² N
Answer: F_max ≈ 4.1 × 10⁻¹² N

blocks.prompt: 10.3 A square coil of side 15 cm each consists of 60 turns. Initially, it is located in a uniform magnetic field of magnitude 0.8 T such that plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field. The coil is then turned through an angle of θ = 30° in a time of 2 s. Determine the average induced emf. (Ans: 0.54 V)
blocks.explanation:
Given: side = 15 cm = 0.15 m, A = (0.15 m)² = 0.0225 m²; N = 60; B = 0.8 T; turned through 30° in Δt = 2 s
Required: average emf ε = ?
Solution:
Plane perpendicular to B means the normal is along B: θ₁ = 0°. After turning, θ₂ = 30°.
φ₁ = BA cos 0° = 0.8 × 0.0225 = 0.0180 Wb
φ₂ = BA cos 30° = 0.0180 × 0.866 = 0.0156 Wb
Δφ = φ₂ − φ₁ = −0.0024 Wb
ε = −N Δφ/Δt = −60 × (−0.0024 Wb)/2 s = 0.072 V
Answer: ε ≈ 0.072 V (7.2 × 10⁻² V)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints 0.54 V. That value is N × BA/Δt = 60 × 0.018/2, the emf if the whole flux disappeared (a turn of 90°). For a turn of 30° the flux falls only from BA to BA cos 30°, so the average emf is 60 × 0.018 × (1 − cos 30°)/2 ≈ 0.072 V.

blocks.prompt: 10.4 A metallic rod is moving through a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T. The emf induced across its ends is found to be 0.8 V. It is required to induce an emf of 2.4 V across its ends. How much field strength is needed for this? (0.6 T)
blocks.explanation:
Given: B₁ = 0.2 T, ε₁ = 0.8 V; ε₂ = 2.4 V; same v and L
Required: B₂ = ?
Solution:
ε = vBL, so ε ∝ B (v and L unchanged)
B₂ = B₁ × ε₂/ε₁ = 0.2 T × 2.4 V/0.8 V = 0.6 T
Answer: B₂ = 0.6 T

blocks.prompt: 10.5 A copper ring has a radius of 4.0 cm and resistance of 1.0 mΩ. A magnetic field is applied over the ring, perpendicular to its plane. If the magnetic field increases from 0.2 T to 0.4 T in a time interval of 5 × 10⁻³ s, what is the current in the ring during this interval? (Ans: 201 A)

10.6 A coil of 10 turns and 35 cm² area is in a perpendicular magnetic field of 0.5 T. The coil is pulled out of the field in 1.0 s. Find the induced emf in the coil as it is pulled out of the field. (Ans: 1.75 × 10⁻² V)
blocks.explanation:
Given: N = 10; A = 35 cm² = 35 × 10⁻⁴ m²; B = 0.5 T; Δt = 1.0 s
Required: ε = ?
Solution:
φ₁ = BA = 0.5 T × 35 × 10⁻⁴ m² = 1.75 × 10⁻³ Wb; φ₂ = 0 (out of the field)
Δφ = −1.75 × 10⁻³ Wb
ε = −N Δφ/Δt = −10 × (−1.75 × 10⁻³ Wb)/1.0 s = 1.75 × 10⁻² V
Answer: ε = 1.75 × 10⁻² V

blocks.prompt: 10.7 A proton is accelerated by a potential difference of 6 × 10⁵ volts. It then enters perpendicularly in a uniform magnetic field B = 1.0 weber m⁻². Find the radius of curvature of the path of the proton. m = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. (Ans: 11.16 cm)
blocks.explanation:
Given: V = 6 × 10⁵ V; B = 1.0 T; m = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C
Required: r = ?
Solution:
Speed: ½mv² = eV
v = √(2eV/m) = √(2 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 6 × 10⁵/1.67 × 10⁻²⁷) = √(1.15 × 10¹⁴) = 1.07 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹
Radius: evB = mv²/r, so
r = mv/(eB) = (1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg)(1.07 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹)/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C × 1.0 T) = 0.112 m
Answer: r ≈ 0.112 m ≈ 11.2 cm (the book's 11.16 cm differs only by rounding)

blocks.prompt: 10.8 A proton enters a uniform magnetic field B = 0.300 weber m⁻² in a direction making an angle 45° with the magnetic field. What will be the radius of the circular path if the velocity of proton is 10⁷ m s⁻¹. (Ans: 2.46 × 10⁻¹ m)
blocks.explanation:
Given: B = 0.300 T; θ = 45°; v = 10⁷ m s⁻¹; m = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C
Required: r = ?
Solution:
Only the velocity component perpendicular to B makes the circle: v⊥ = v sin 45°.
v⊥ = 10⁷ × 0.707 = 7.07 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹
r = m v⊥/(eB) = (1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg)(7.07 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹)/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C × 0.300 T) = 0.246 m
Answer: r = 0.246 m = 2.46 × 10⁻¹ m

blocks.prompt: 10.9 Three identical conducting rods L₁, L₂ and L₃ are moving in different planes with the same speeds v₁ = v₂ = v₃ = 2.5 m s⁻¹ as shown in the figure. The length of each rod is 60 cm. A constant magnetic field of magnitude B = 0.5 T is directed along z-axis. Find the magnitude of emf induced in each rod and indicate which end of the rod is positive. [(Rod L₁) emf = 0.75 V, and end a, (Rod L₂) emf = 0 (Rod L₃) emf = 0)]. [Figure: B along +z. Rod L₁ lies along the x-axis (end a towards the origin, end b towards +x) and moves along +y with v₁. Rod L₂ lies along the x-axis and moves along +z with v₂. Rod L₃ lies along the y-axis (end a towards the origin, end b towards +y) and moves along +z with v₃.]
blocks.explanation:
Given: v = 2.5 m s⁻¹; L = 60 cm = 0.60 m; B = 0.5 T along +z
Required: emf in each rod and its positive end
Solution:
Rod L₁: v (along y), B (along z) and the rod (along x) are mutually perpendicular:
ε₁ = vBL = 2.5 m s⁻¹ × 0.5 T × 0.60 m = 0.75 V
Force on positive charges F = q v × B: ŷ × ẑ = x̂, so they are pushed along +x, to end b. End b is positive (end a negative).
Rod L₂: v is along z, parallel to B, so v × B = 0: ε₂ = vBL sin 0° = 0.
Rod L₃: v is also along z, parallel to B: ε₃ = 0.
Answer: L₁: 0.75 V (positive end b by F = q v × B); L₂: 0; L₃: 0

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book names end a of rod L₁ as the positive end. With v₁ along +y and B along +z, the force on positive charges is q v × B along +x, towards end b as drawn, so b is the positive end; electrons collect at a, which is the negative end. The magnitudes (0.75 V, 0, 0) are right.

blocks.prompt: 10.10 An emf of 0.5 V is induced across the ends of a metal rod moving through a magnetic field of 0.4 T. If an emf of 1.5 V has to be induced, what field strength would be needed for that? Assume that all other factors remain the same. (Ans: 1.2 T)
blocks.explanation:
Given: ε₁ = 0.5 V at B₁ = 0.4 T; ε₂ = 1.5 V
Required: B₂ = ?
Solution:
ε = vBL, so ε ∝ B
B₂ = B₁ × ε₂/ε₁ = 0.4 T × 1.5 V/0.5 V = 1.2 T
Answer: B₂ = 1.2 T

blocks.prompt: 7.11 A charged particle moves through a velocity selector at a constant velocity of 4.96 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹ in a direction perpendicular to both E and B. If the magnetic field strength is 0.114 T, what should be the magnitude of electric field intensity so that the particle moves undeflected? (Ans: 5.65 × 10³ N C⁻¹)
blocks.explanation:
Given: v = 4.96 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹; B = 0.114 T
Required: E = ?
Solution:
For no deflection qE = qvB, so
E = vB = (4.96 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹)(0.114 T) = 5.65 × 10³ N C⁻¹
Answer: E = 5.65 × 10³ N C⁻¹

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The last two problems are printed as 7.11 and 7.12; in this chapter they are 10.11 and 10.12. In 7.11 the × sign is missing in "4.96 10⁴ m s⁻¹"; it is 4.96 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

blocks.prompt: 7.12 A current-carrying conductor PQ of length 2 m is placed perpendicularly to a magnetic field of flux density 0.5 T as shown in the figure. The resulting force on the conductor is 1 N acting into the plane of the paper. What is the magnitude and direction of the current? (Ans: 1 A, Q to P) [Figure: the field B points to the right across the page; the conductor PQ is vertical, with P at the top and Q at the bottom.]
blocks.explanation:
Given: L = 2 m; B = 0.5 T (to the right); F = 1 N (into the paper); conductor perpendicular to B
Required: I = ? and its direction
Solution:
F = BIL sin 90°
I = F/(BL) = 1 N/(0.5 T × 2 m) = 1 A
Direction from F = I L × B: with B to the right (x̂), a current upward from Q to P (ŷ) gives ŷ × x̂ = −ẑ, i.e., into the paper, as stated. So the current flows from Q to P.
(Check with Fleming's left-hand rule: first finger to the right along B, thumb into the paper, the second finger points up the page, from Q to P.)
Answer: I = 1 A, from Q to P
